sentences.text: Waimanu likely had the body shape of a flightless loon or diver and may have moved like the great auk. Although it was probably flightless with wings specialized for diving, its wing bones lacked the extreme aquatic adaptations seen in modern penguins.

The genus name Waimanu is derived from the Māori words for "water" and "bird," while the species Waimanu manneringi was named in honor of Al Mannering, who discovered and collected the holotype specimen.

Waimanu was discovered in 1980 in the Basal Waipara Greensand near the Waipara River in Canterbury, New Zealand, and the holotype specimen is currently held at the Canterbury Museum in Christchurch, New Zealand.
The holotype is a partial skeleton containing an almost complete right tibiotarsus, part of a fibula, a tarsometatarsus, a pelvis, a synsacrum, and four tail vertebrae.
Waimanu is a genus of primitive penguin that lived shortly after the Cretaceous-Tertiary mass extinction and belongs to the order Sphenisciformes, which includes modern penguins.
The genus Waimanu was described by Jones, Ando, and Fordyce in 2006 and includes the type species W. manneringi and the species W. tuatahi.

Waimanu lived during the Paleocene epoch, approximately 62 to 60 million years ago, shortly after the Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event. Waimanu manneringi lived in the mid-Paleocene, approximately 61 million years ago, while Waimanu tuatahi lived in the late Paleocene, perhaps around 58 million years ago.
Waimanu lived from the Selandian to the Thanetian stages, between 61.66 and 56 million years ago.

Waimanu provides evidence for the debate regarding whether modern birds (Neoaves) radiated before or immediately after the extinction of non-avian dinosaurs. The discovery of Waimanu supports the idea that Neoaves radiated either shortly before the extinction of non-avian dinosaurs or extremely rapidly afterward in geological terms.
